name: Self-Play and Quality-Diversity for Diverse Play Generation
key_paper: Felten, F., Talbi, E.-G., & Danoy, G. (2023). Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Quality-Diversity. arXiv:2306.14467. Also foundational: Mouret, J.-B., & Clune, J. (2015). Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites. arXiv:1504.04909.
algorithm_description: Quality-Diversity (QD) methods, most notably MAP-Elites, maintain a structured archive of solutions (plays) that are both high-performing (quality) and behaviorally diverse (coverage across a user-defined feature space). In the RL formulation (QD-RL), multiple actor heads or population members are each rewarded for two objectives: (1) maximizing cumulative return (hit quality) and (2) occupying a unique behavioral cell in a discretized behavior descriptor space (e.g., number-range distribution, parity pattern, hot-cold balance). Self-play extends this by having actor heads compete or collaborate — each head is evaluated relative to the outputs of other heads, with diversity bonuses penalizing overlap between simultaneously generated plays. At each generation, new solutions are produced by mutating archive elites, evaluated for fitness and behavior descriptor, then inserted into the archive if they outperform the current occupant of their cell or fill an empty cell. The result is a large, diverse population of non-dominated solutions rather than a single best policy.
action_space_handling: QD methods treat the combinatorial action space (choose k from N) via population-level diversity rather than per-step diversity. Each individual actor in the population uses a standard discrete policy (softmax over N logits, with autoregressive masking or Gumbel-top-k for constraint enforcement). Diversity is imposed at the population level: the archive structure forces different actors to occupy different regions of behavior space. Self-play variants add pairwise diversity rewards: actor i receives a penalty proportional to the set-intersection overlap with actors j != i, pushing them apart in number space. This is orthogonal to and composable with any single-actor action-space mechanism (autoregressive, flat multi-hot, pointer network).
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: Each actor head in the population generates a play using the same k-of-N sampling mechanism as a standard actor — typically autoregressive masking (select number 1 from N logits, mask it, select number 2 from remaining N-1, etc.) or Gumbel-top-k joint sampling. The QD/self-play layer operates above this: (1) M actor heads run in parallel, each producing one play per forward pass; (2) a pairwise diversity matrix is computed (Jaccard distance or set intersection count between all M*M pairs); (3) each actor's reward is augmented with a diversity bonus proportional to its uniqueness score; (4) actors that collapse to the same play are penalized and their parameters are perturbed (mutation) or re-initialized. The archive (MAP-Elites grid) bins plays by behavioral descriptors (e.g., mean number value, number of odd/even balls) and retains the highest-reward play per bin.
sequential_generation_strategy: QD and self-play operate at the population level and are agnostic to the within-actor generation strategy. Each individual actor can use joint (flat multi-hot), autoregressive (one number at a time with masking), or flow-based generation. For the lottery-nn project, autoregressive masking is recommended within each actor head, as it guarantees exactly k distinct numbers without post-hoc filtering. The QD diversity mechanism acts on the output plays (sets of k numbers) rather than on the generation trajectory, so it composes cleanly with any sequential strategy. Inter-number correlations can be modeled within each actor's autoregressive pass; inter-play diversity is enforced by the QD population mechanism.
gradient_estimator_type: Within each actor, standard REINFORCE (score function estimator) or its variance-reduced variants (RLOO, REINFORCE with leave-one-out baseline) are used. The diversity bonus is typically non-differentiable (set intersection is discrete), so it enters the reward signal rather than the gradient directly — no additional estimator is needed if the base policy uses REINFORCE. When differentiable diversity is desired, a soft Jaccard similarity (computed via soft top-k relaxations such as NeuralSort or Gumbel-top-k) can be included in the loss, enabling straight-through or reparameterization gradients for the diversity term. In MAP-Elites specifically, gradient information is not used at all — evolution (mutation + selection) drives search, making it gradient-free. Gradient-based QD variants (DQD, CMA-MEGA) use the gradient of a surrogate fitness function to guide archive exploration.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Each actor enforces the k-of-N constraint independently, using the same mechanisms available to single-actor policies: (1) Autoregressive masking — most common in practice, masks already-selected numbers at each of k steps, guaranteeing distinct selection. (2) Gumbel-top-k — joint sampling without replacement in one forward pass. (3) Rejection sampling with replacement — simplest but biased. The QD/self-play layer adds no new constraint complexity — it operates on completed, constraint-satisfying plays. The archive behavioral descriptor computation (e.g., binning by mean ball value) also operates on valid plays only, so constraint enforcement is fully decoupled from diversity enforcement.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium. QD methods are more sample-efficient than single-policy RL in the sense that the archive retains all good solutions found during training — no solution is discarded due to policy updates (unlike on-policy PPO). However, MAP-Elites in its classic form is evolutionary and requires many fitness evaluations to fill the archive, which is expensive when each evaluation requires a real lottery draw. In the offline setting (100-200 historical draws), QD methods can be adapted by: (1) using the historical draws as a fixed evaluator (scoring each generated play against past draws for hit count); (2) training M actor heads jointly on the fixed dataset with a diversity augmented reward. The multi-actor diversity bonus is computed cheaply from generated plays without requiring new environment interactions. Sample efficiency is medium — better than naive random search, competitive with single-actor REINFORCE on small data, but not as theoretically grounded as offline RL methods with conservative value estimation.
regularization_built_in: Several regularization mechanisms are inherent: (1) Archive-based selection pressure — only the best solution per behavioral cell survives, preventing the population from collapsing to a single attractor. (2) Diversity reward — the explicit penalty for inter-actor overlap acts as a regularizer against degenerate generation. (3) Entropy bonus within each actor — standard entropy regularization prevents any single actor from becoming deterministic. (4) Population-level implicit regularization — maintaining M diverse actors makes it unlikely that all M overfit identically to the small training set; the diversity pressure forces different actors to explore different regions, effectively acting as an ensemble regularizer. (5) Mutation/perturbation in evolutionary QD variants adds noise that prevents premature convergence.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: Key failure modes on n < 200: (1) Archive underfilling — with sparse reward (95% zero-hit plays), very few solutions achieve non-zero fitness scores, leaving most archive cells empty and the diversity mechanism ineffective. (2) Behavioral descriptor collapse — if the descriptors are not well-chosen, many plays map to the same cell regardless of actual numerical diversity (e.g., using only mean ball value bins all moderate-range plays to the same cell). (3) Diversity without quality — QD can produce many diverse but equally poor plays; on small data, the quality signal is too weak to guide the diversity-quality tradeoff. (4) M-actor overhead on small datasets — training M=5-10 actor heads on 100-200 draws can lead to each actor overfitting its diversity niche rather than finding genuinely better predictions. (5) Self-play instability — if actor heads are trained adversarially (each trying to avoid the others' outputs), the training dynamics can become non-stationary and diverge on small data.

data_regime_evidence.minimum_training_samples_tested: [uncertain] — MAP-Elites and QD-RL papers (Mouret & Clune 2015, Colas et al. 2020 QD-RL) primarily report results on continuous control tasks (robotics, locomotion) with thousands to millions of evaluation steps. The Felten et al. 2023 QD-MORL paper uses standard MO-RL benchmarks (MO-MuJoCo, MO-Highway) which require thousands of episodes. No published evaluation of QD methods on static datasets of < 200 labeled samples for combinatorial discrete outputs has been found.
data_regime_evidence.performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain] — No published curve for QD diversity quality vs. dataset size in the 50-200 range for combinatorial outputs. The diversity mechanism (set intersection penalty) is independent of dataset size for a given set of generated plays, but the quality signal degradation follows the same curve as single-actor REINFORCE on sparse rewards.
data_regime_evidence.comparison_baseline: [uncertain] — QD methods have not been directly compared against single-actor REINFORCE or bandit methods on datasets of < 200 combinatorial samples in the published literature as of 2025.

convergence_guarantees_small_n: MAP-Elites has theoretical guarantees only in the evolutionary sense: it will eventually fill all reachable archive cells if given sufficient evaluations (completeness guarantee under mild regularity, Doncieux et al. 2019). For gradient-based QD-RL variants, convergence results follow from the underlying policy gradient theory and are asymptotic. No finite-sample convergence bounds exist for QD methods in the n < 200 regime. In practice, the archive-based retention property provides a monotone improvement guarantee for quality within each cell (solutions can only be replaced by better solutions), which is a weak but useful convergence property absent in on-policy RL. The diversity coverage is not guaranteed to converge at any specific rate.
reward_distribution_handling: QD methods handle sparse rewards better than single-policy RL in one key respect: the archive retains any solution that achieves non-zero fitness, no matter how rare. In a lottery setting with 95% zero-hit plays, a QD archive will preserve any play that ever matches 1+ numbers, and population pressure ensures these rare successes are used as parents for further search. However, QD does not address the fundamental sparsity problem — if no play in the initial population achieves non-zero reward, the archive remains empty and diversity provides no advantage over random generation. Reward shaping (hit count / k as continuous reward) is recommended to smooth the landscape. Minimum draws for stable QD learning: [uncertain] — empirically similar to single-actor REINFORCE; perhaps 50-100 draws to provide sufficient quality signal for meaningful archive filling.
credit_assignment_granularity: Standard QD methods assign reward at the play level (how many numbers matched the draw). Number-level (semi-bandit) feedback can be incorporated by using per-number hit indicators to define the behavioral descriptor rather than the reward — for example, a behavioral descriptor could be (number of low-range hits, number of high-range hits), turning per-number feedback into a structured diversity signal. This is a creative extension not standard in the QD literature but well-suited to the lottery domain. Within each actor, the REINFORCE gradient uses play-level reward by default; reward decomposition into per-number signals requires architectural changes (M separate binary critics, one per number) that are feasible but add complexity.
diversity_mechanism: Diversity is the defining feature of QD methods and operates through multiple complementary mechanisms: (1) MAP-Elites archive — the behavior space (e.g., fraction of odd numbers, mean ball value, hot/cold ball balance) is discretized into a grid; only one solution occupies each cell, forcing the population to spread across the space. (2) Explicit diversity reward in self-play variants — each actor i receives a reward bonus proportional to the minimum pairwise set distance to all other actors: bonus_i = min_{j != i} (1 - |S_i intersect S_j| / k), where S_i and S_j are the sets of numbers in plays i and j. (3) Novelty search as surrogate fitness — in novelty-based QD, actors are rewarded purely for producing plays that differ from all previously seen plays, with quality only used as a secondary selection criterion. (4) Population replacement policy — solutions are only replaced by strictly better solutions in their cell, ensuring diversity is maintained across generations even if overall quality decreases.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: QD methods are partially compatible with offline training but were originally designed for online evolutionary search. Key considerations: (1) The archive quality signal requires evaluating generated plays against an environment (a draw) — in offline mode, generated plays can be scored against historical draws (semi-bandit feedback), computing the hit count for each historical draw and averaging. This is a valid offline adaptation. (2) The evolutionary mutation operators (perturbing actor network weights) do not require environment interaction, only fitness evaluation — compatible with offline historical data. (3) Self-play diversity bonuses are computed purely from generated plays (set intersection), requiring zero environment interaction — fully offline compatible. (4) Gradient-based QD (DQD, CMA-MEGA) requires gradient of fitness w.r.t. policy parameters — compatible with offline RL if a differentiable surrogate fitness (learned critic) is used. Verdict: QD diversity mechanisms are offline-compatible; quality signal requires offline evaluation against historical draws, which is feasible. More offline-friendly than PPO but less principled than conservative offline RL methods.
key_dependencies: PyTorch (already present). Optional: qdax (https://github.com/adaptive-intelligent-robotics/QDax) — JAX-based QD library, not PyTorch-native but provides MAP-Elites reference. ribs (https://github.com/icaros-usc/pyribs) — Python library for MAP-Elites and QD algorithms, framework-agnostic, PyTorch-compatible for neural policy evaluation. No mandatory new dependencies if implementing core self-play diversity reward from scratch — only requires standard PyTorch tensor operations for set intersection computation.
estimated_lines_of_code: 400-600 lines of new code: M-actor ensemble wrapper (~80 lines), pairwise set-intersection diversity reward computation (~60 lines), archive (MAP-Elites grid) data structure with behavioral descriptor binning (~120 lines), diversity-augmented training loop integrating with existing REINFORCE or bandit (~100 lines), behavioral descriptor extraction from generated plays (~60 lines), population management (archive insert/replace logic, ~80 lines), evaluation utilities comparing archive coverage metrics (~60 lines). Excludes boilerplate. Simpler self-play-only variant (no archive, just pairwise diversity reward) requires ~200 lines.
transfer_learning_compatibility: High. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder serves as the shared backbone for all M actor heads — each head is a small linear layer on top of the shared encoder output, initialized identically and then diversified through training. The lottery_id embedding already handles per-lottery differentiation, so the same multi-actor architecture applies to all three lotteries simultaneously. The pretrained encoder provides a strong initialization that allows actor heads to start from a meaningful representation rather than random features, significantly accelerating archive filling. Transfer is especially beneficial here: the shared encoder has already learned temporal draw patterns across all three lotteries, so diversity pressure at the actor-head level will produce plays that are both meaningfully diverse and grounded in real statistical patterns.
specific_application_in_project: QD self-play would be used in Phase 2 as the primary diversity mechanism for play generation across all three lotteries. Concrete implementation: (1) Replace the current single-actor temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py with an M=5 actor ensemble (one actor head per desired play per call). (2) Each actor head is a 2-layer MLP on top of the SharedLotteryTransformer encoder output, outputting N logits (N=50 for LottoMax/6-49, N=49 for Daily Grand); autoregressive masking samples exactly k numbers. (3) After generating M plays per lottery per round, compute a pairwise diversity matrix (set intersection counts) and augment each actor's training reward: reward_i = hit_count_i / k + lambda * diversity_bonus_i, where lambda=0.3 is a tunable weight. (4) A lightweight MAP-Elites archive bins plays by two behavioral descriptors: (a) fraction of numbers in the low third of the pool (1-17 for LottoMax), (b) count of numbers in the top third (34-50). This 3x3 grid forces coverage of low/mid/high number regions. (5) After each real draw, all M actors are updated using REINFORCE with the diversity-augmented reward; the archive is updated with the current best plays per cell. (6) The bandit.py Thompson sampling selects which archive cell to draw predictions from at inference time. This replaces temperature-softmax in predict.py and extends bandit.py with archive-aware cell selection.
replaces_or_extends: Extends temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py by replacing single-actor generation with an M-actor ensemble with pairwise diversity reward. Extends bandit.py with archive-aware Thompson sampling over behavioral descriptor cells. Does not replace the SharedLotteryTransformer backbone — adds actor heads on top of the existing encoder.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. pyribs (https://github.com/icaros-usc/pyribs) — Python MAP-Elites library, framework-agnostic, well-maintained, supports custom fitness functions and behavioral descriptors; integrates with PyTorch policy evaluation via callback. 2. QDax (https://github.com/adaptive-intelligent-robotics/QDax) — JAX-based QD library from InstaDeep/ISAE-SUPAERO, includes MAP-Elites, CVT-MAP-Elites, and QD-PG (gradient-based); not PyTorch-native but algorithms are portable. 3. QD-RL reference implementations from Colas et al. 2020 (https://github.com/flowersteam/qdrl) — combines QD archive with standard RL policy gradient, Python/PyTorch. 4. Self-play diversity in multi-agent RL: OpenAI Five and AlphaStar use self-play for agent diversity; code not fully open-source, but algorithmic details published. 5. Felten et al. 2023 QD-MORL code: [uncertain] — code availability for the specific Felten et al. 2023 paper not confirmed as of knowledge cutoff.
benchmark_results: MAP-Elites (Mouret & Clune 2015): originally demonstrated on robot locomotion morphology search — archives of 13,000+ diverse locomotion strategies found vs. single-solution optimization finding 1. QD-RL (Colas et al. 2020, Nilsson & Cully 2021): applied to continuous control (HalfCheetah, Ant locomotion) — QD-RL fills 60-80% of behavioral archive cells vs. 5-15% for pure reward maximization, with no statistically significant quality degradation vs. best single-policy RL. Felten et al. 2023 QD-MORL: achieves 2-3x improvement in hypervolume coverage of the Pareto front on MO-MuJoCo benchmarks vs. standard MORL baselines. Self-play diversity bonus: Jaderberg et al. (2019) Capture the Flag — population-based self-play with diversity reward produces qualitatively more diverse strategies than single-agent training; direct metric comparison not combinatorial. No published benchmark on discrete combinatorial k-of-N outputs with n < 200 samples.
notable_use_cases: 1. Robot morphology and locomotion search (original MAP-Elites application) — find 1000s of diverse locomotion strategies across terrain/body-shape behavior space; structural similarity: combinatorial discrete choices (joint angles, morphology), archive-based diversity. 2. Game AI diversity (OpenAI Five, AlphaStar, Capture the Flag) — self-play populations produce diverse strategies resistant to exploitation; structural similarity: multiple solution diversity, competitive quality-diversity tradeoff. 3. Drug/molecule design with QD — maintaining diverse chemical scaffolds while maximizing binding affinity; structural similarity: discrete combinatorial selection (atoms, bonds), sparse reward (assay results), small validated set. 4. Combinatorial optimization with QD (Vassiliades & Mouret 2018, QD for TSP) — MAP-Elites applied to vehicle routing to find diverse high-quality route families; directly analogous combinatorial structure. 5. Recommendation slate diversity — self-play diversity rewards for generating non-redundant item sets in recommender systems; directly analogous k-of-N combinatorial structure with explicit diversity requirement.
